new_statements.quote: All of the languages of this area (Mangarrayi, Ngalakgan, Ngandi, Alawa, Marra and Warndarrang) have a series of prefixes for person and/or gender [...] Again, while the placenames often have the right morphology and prosody (stress on the stem) to be prefixed words, often the stem cannot be identified with a meaning. [...] The stress in nya-Marranguru, falling on the first syllable of the noun stem, is the characteristic stress pattern of nouns with polysyllabic stems in all the languages of the Roper (see Baker 1999). Its retention in the placename indicates that the word is not opaque to speakers: stress is normally initial in unprefixed stems in Marra.
new_statements.citation: Baker, Brett. 2002. "'I'm going to where-her-brisket-is': placenames in the Roper." In Luise Hercus, Flavia Hodges & Jane Simpson (eds), The Land is a Map: Placenames of Indigenous Origin in Australia, 103-129. Canberra: Pandanus Books / ANU E Press.
new_statements.locator: §6.2 'Prefixes on names', p. 125 (see also fn. 24, p. 115)
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences

new_statements.rule_in_words: In the Roper River languages, Ngandi named among them, primary stress falls on the first syllable of a polysyllabic noun stem; class/person prefixes are skipped (stress on the stem, not the prefix). In unprefixed stems stress is therefore word-initial.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed for Ngandi. (Merlan 1983:30 for sister language Ngalakan: four-syllable roots mostly 1st + secondary 3rd; Baker 2008 snippet: Ngalakgan stress 'is initial, as in words in general'.)
new_statements.exceptions: Statement restricted to nouns with polysyllabic stems; Baker 2002 gives no Ngandi examples (all illustrated forms are Marra/Ngalakgan placenames). Vowel length exists in 'a handful of stems' in Ngandi (Baker 2008 snippet) — interaction with stress unknown.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (prefixed noun word; stress on stem-initial syllable). A regional generalisation by a Gunwinyguan specialist citing his own thesis (Baker 1999), not a description of Ngandi data; Heath 1978, the only reference grammar, appears to contain no stress statement (full-text index of the scan has no hit for stress/accent/pitch vocabulary).
new_statements.identity_note: Language-level Ngandi (ngan1295); Baker 2002's statement covers 'all the languages of the Roper' (Mangarrayi, Ngalakgan, Ngandi, Alawa, Marra, Warndarrang) and is illustrated with Marra and Ngalakgan placenames, not Ngandi forms. Heath 1978 = Glottolog hhtype grammar_sketch; the OL/IA scan is the Trent University copy.

sources.note: p.125 §6.2: lists Ngandi among 'all of the languages of this area (Mangarrayi, Ngalakgan, Ngandi, Alawa, Marra and Warndarrang)' whose prefixed words carry 'stress on the stem'; 'stress... falling on the first syllable of the noun stem, is the characteristic stress pattern of nouns with polysyllabic stems in all the languages of the Roper (see Baker 1999)'. fn.24 p.115: the verb wawurlu 'always takes a stress on the first syllable' in compound placenames (Marra data). Regional generalisation, not a Ngandi-specific description.
